title: Autoscale-aware reservation negotiation and throughput forecast playflow
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem statement: Customers are requesting reservation commitments with guaranteed throughput but expect autoscaling flexibility and transparent cost trade-offs. Current intake/approval flows treat reserved throughput and autoscale policies as separate artifacts, causing manual negotiation overhead and mismatches between committed throughput and runtime autoscale behavior. Goal: design a straight-through playflow that produces a reservation decision (approve / require modifications / reject) using a combined forecast + autoscale template that ensures throughput guarantees can be met by fleet controls, optionally with staged probabilistic buffers.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Intake form returns a recommended autoscale template and estimated monthly token cost for the requested committed throughput; 2) Approval lanes (auto-approve / sales-review / exec-review) selected automatically based on predicted utilization, customer tier and risk score; 3) System runs a preflight simulation that flags potential SLO violations given historical workload shapes and proposed autoscale policy; 4) Approved reservations emit a binding autoscale profile attached to the fleet allocation so runtime can enforce graceful fallback and cost controls; 5) Audit log and notification hooks for ops and sales are created at approval time.
notes: Key trade-offs: a) Tight guarantees require more conservative buffer or reserved spare nodes, which increases cost to Redwood; b) Allowing aggressive autoscaling for bursty workloads reduces unit cost but weakens guarantee semantics — need a clear guardrail and billing model; c) For enterprise customers we can offer tiered guarantee SLAs (e.g., 99.9 latency/throughput vs 95.0) with corresponding autoscale profiles and pricing.
proposed_solution: 1) Intake scorer: extend current capacity-intake scorer to evaluate requested throughput across 3 axes — steady-state tokens/sec, peak percentile (95/99), and KV cache hit assumptions. 2) Autoscale template generator: produce one of three templates (Conservative, Balanced, Elastic) with explicit min/max nodes, warm-hot buffer, and a probabilistic buffer multiplier for very bursty periods. 3) Preflight simulator: run a 24/7 simulated dispatch using customer's historical sample traces (or synthetic if none) to compute risk of overload and expected costs. 4) Straight-through rules: if risk < 5% and customer tier in {self-serve, growth}, auto-approve; if risk 5-20% then route to Sales/Capacity team for negotiation; if >20% require architecture review. 5) Approval outputs: approved reservations produce (a) fleet allocation request, (b) an attached autoscale profile that the runtime will honor and (c) a rollback/fallback policy linking to compatible model variants or degraded latency tiers.
implementation_notes: Engineering work will span: API changes to the reservation intake endpoint, scoring model updates, simulator service, and a UI step in Console for review/override. Also runtime needs a small enhancement to attach a reservation profile to fleet assignments and expose enforced min capacity and probabilistic buffer behavior. We should coordinate with Billing to ensure billing primitives can represent combined reserved+burst capacity pricing.
risks_and_mitigations: - Risk: Simulator false negatives due to poor trace sampling. Mitigation: require conservative defaults when sample size < threshold and surface confidence level. - Risk: Customers will ask for hard guarantees but provide unrealistic traffic patterns. Mitigation: include an explicit runnable SLA calculator in the intake email and require acceptance. - Risk: Runtime enforcement complexity. Mitigation: iterate with a beta group and keep a manual override for ops during rollout.
outstanding_questions: What percentile window should we use for peak (95 vs 99) as the canonical signal for approval?
Should committed throughput billing be split into steady reservation + burst pool metered separately?
Which Sales tiers can auto-approve (we propose self-serve + growth) and which require manual review?
Do we need KMS audit hooks when attaching autoscale profiles for Private deployments?
